warmup.text: Before you write, read the poem on the Poetry Corner card out loud three ways: flat, too fast, and the way you think it should sound. That last reading is the one you are practicing for.

words.text: Today the word work points at your own writing. You edit your Reader's Portrait, match four roots to their meanings, and hunt for misspellings. Then light five more stops on the year's map.

reading.text: Pick a short passage from one of your two novels, the one you will quote in your letter. Copy it exactly, mark where you will pause, and read it aloud three times. Then read the card about a real letter from the Gold Rush.

assignment.text: Draft your whole letter today. Start with Dear future fifth grader, then your Reader's Portrait, your claim, two reasons with a moment from each book, one fair point, and your closing.

readnow.text: No new chapter today. Pick a passage to read aloud, then draft your letter.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you work. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Proof from both books is what makes a recommendation believable.
how.use: You will use it in your letter's two reasons.

do: Read the first sentence. It is correct.
Write the second sentence correctly in your reading journal.
Tap See the Answer to check.
how.why: Fixing one sentence at a time trains your eye for your own letter.

do: Read the question.
Write 2 or 3 sentences in your reading journal.
Then go on.
how.why: Thinking first gives you something to say in your letter.

do: Read the poem out loud three times.
Read the tip.
Answer the question in your reading journal.
how.why: Reading a poem aloud shows what you understood: where it slows down and where it rushes.

do: Read the checklist.
Edit your Reader’s Portrait with it.
Write the edited version in the box.
how.why: Your portrait opens your letter, so it should be your cleanest writing.

do: Read each word.
Tap the root and meaning that match it.
Then do the journal task.
how.why: Matching a root to its meaning is how you read a word nobody taught you.

do: Read the short draft.
Find the misspelled words.
Then check your own letter draft in your reading journal.
how.why: Finding mistakes in someone else's writing trains you to find them in yours.

do: Read Pick, Mark, Practice.
Answer the three questions, one box at a time.
how.why: A quote you can read well is a quote a new reader will remember.

do: Read how your letter goes, from greeting to closing.
Draft your whole letter in the box.
how.why: Getting it all down first gives you something to revise.

cards.title: Real history: letters that crossed time
cards.intro: Real letters can outlive the people who wrote them. Here is one from the Gold Rush.

items.meaning: Louise Clappe, who signed her letters “Dame Shirley.” In 1851 and 1852 she lived in two mining camps on the Feather River in California and wrote 23 letters to her sister Molly in Massachusetts.

items.term: Her goodbye to the mining camp
items.meaning: She wrote this when she had to leave. Barbarous means rough and wild.
items.line: My heart is heavy at the thought of departing forever from this place. I like this wild and barbarous life. I leave it with regret.
items.cite: Letter the Twenty-third, Indian Bar, November 1852

items.term: Why we can still read it
items.meaning: Her letters were printed in The Pioneer, a San Francisco magazine, in 1854 and 1855, and in books ever since. A letter written for one reader reached readers for more than 170 years.

cards.note: Source: The Shirley Letters from California Mines in 1851-52, edited by Thomas C. Russell (1922), on the Internet Archive. Your letter is written for one new reader too.

game.title: The Year's Map
game.sub: This week's word game · 5 stops today
game.look: A map of your whole year: five stops, one for each novel's world, from Wethersfield to San Francisco. Each clue asks for a word built from a root you learned while you read that book. A right answer lights the stop.

do: Read the clue.
Tap the word that fits.
A right word lights the stop. Then tap On to the next stop.
how.why: Every root you learned this year still works. Here you use one from each book.

game.doneLine: Come back next lesson to light the map again with new words.

rounds.clue: Which word names old-fashioned glasses that help you see?
rounds.why: spect means look or see. Spectacles help you see.
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

rounds.clue: Which word names something a person says will happen?
rounds.why: dict means say. A prediction is said before it happens.
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

rounds.clue: Which word names the true story of a person's life, written by someone else?
rounds.why: graph means write and bio means life: a written life.
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

rounds.clue: Which word means you cannot see it?
rounds.why: vis means see, and in- means not.
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

rounds.clue: Which word means to pull back, or take back words you said?
rounds.why: tract means pull. To retract is to pull back.
rounds.miss: Look for the root in the clue's meaning.

virtue.name: wisdom
virtue.title: Wisdom in the year's books
virtue.intro: Tap the moment from this year's novels that you think shows the most wisdom.

options.t: Kit keeps visiting Hannah Tupper when the town turns against her (The Witch of Blackbird Pond).
Nat: “when you depend on a book and it has a mistake, you’d have been safer not depending on it” (Carry On, Mr. Bowditch, Chapter 22).
James Otis: “we fight, we die, for a simple thing. Only that a man can stand up” (Johnny Tremain, Chapter 8).
Isaac, on the very first page: “Be careful what you wish for” (How I Became a Ghost, Chapter 1).

art.title: Man Writing a Letter
art.alt: A painting of a young man with long hair sitting at a table by a window, writing a letter with a quill pen. A patterned rug covers the table and a framed painting hangs on the wall.
art.look: Gabriël Metsu painted this man writing a letter in the Netherlands around 1665. Look at his face: he is choosing every word. Today you draft your own letter.
